    > **First interior structure found (2026-08-14), `c64-compic-format.md` §5.** The
    > single-class 162-byte body partitions as **`72 | 72 | 18`**, measured three ways:
    > - **Period 72**, at **3.37×** a closed-form permutation null — and **lag 81 scores 0.71×,
    >   *below* its own null**, which directly refutes the natural "two 81-byte screen+colour
    >   maps" reading by analogy with the solved fixed-size `PIC` (570 + 570).
    > - The periodicity is **bounded**: `body[i]==body[i+72]` runs 0.12–0.87 for `i < 72` and
    >   collapses to ≤0.04 past 144, so the relation is exactly `body[0:72] ↔ body[72:144]`.
    > - The two blocks are **planes of the same picture**, not duplicates: 0.415 within a file
    >   vs **0.156** across an exhaustive all-pairs cross-file null (**2.66×**), never identical
    >   in any of 229 bodies, with the 18-byte tail at chance (0.014) as the control.
    >
    > **REFUTED the same day, by rendering:** `72 = 9 cells × 8 bytes` makes `144 + 18` read as
    > 9×2 cells of bitmap plus one colour byte per cell — arithmetically exact for every size
    > class (`162n = 144n + 18n`), and the colour region's histogram even shows the `FB/0B`,
    > `FA/0A` high-nibble-dirty signature the solved `PIC` colour map has. Nine COMPICs, three
    > size classes, both hires and multicolour: **all noise.** The measurement stands; the
    > interpretation of the 72 does not.
    >
    > So the target for the next attempt is sharper than "find the blit": find a blit that
    > consumes **two 72-byte blocks plus an 18-byte tail**. And any future layout proposal must
    > clear the §5.1 null *and* be rendered and looked at before it is written down as solved.
    >
    > **That sharper search was then run, and is a clean NEGATIVE (`c64-compic-format.md` §5.6,
    > pinned by `test_no_code_like_file_carries_both_a_72_loop_and_an_18_loop`).** Scanning all
    > **446 code-like files** in all seven titles for *counted loops* — a constant plus an actual
    > branch, which is what separates a loop bound from an incidental constant:
    > | loop length | hits |
    > | ---: | --- |
    > | 162 (whole body) | **0 anywhere** |
    > | 72 (one block) | 2, both in Pool of Radiance `POOLRA` |
    > | 144 (both blocks) | 2, `SPELLN64` in two titles |
    > | 18 (tail) | 20, scattered |
    >
    > No file anywhere carries both a 72-loop and an 18-loop. It also names a false positive:
    > `GDRIVE01` carries `LDA #$48` and `LDA #$12` five bytes apart at identical offsets in **all
    > seven titles**, reading exactly like block-length-then-tail-length — but they are
    > `STA $C093` / `STA $C094`, the low and high bytes of the single 16-bit constant `$1248`
    > staged for the `$C449` address-copy routine.
    >
    > ⚠️ **CORRECTED the same day (`c64-compic-format.md` §5.7).** Every number above is right;
    > the claim that the zeros *mean* anything was not. Measuring the baseline the negative was
    > never compared against — 4,076 counted loops corpus-wide, **66.1% of bounds below 32** —
    > refutes two of the three headline statements:
    > - **Zero at 162 is not evidence.** In the window 150–174 there are 16 counted loops total
    >   and **16 of the 24 non-162 values are also exactly zero**. Any 162-byte format shows this.
    > - **"No file carries both" is arithmetic.** Exactly **one** file corpus-wide has a 72-loop,
    >   so expected co-occurrence is `1x17/446 = 0.038` files. And 43.5% of all value pairs
    >   co-occur in zero files — zero is the *modal* outcome.
    > - **The surviving hits are CBM constants.** The corpus's most-shared counted loop is
    >   `PIC64`'s `CPY #$12` at body offset 130, byte-identical in all seven titles — but it sits
    >   in a **1541 directory scan** (`CMP #$82` entry type, `CPX #$08` entries/sector, `ADC #$20`
    >   entry size), so its 18 is a *filename* length. Same failure as GDRIVE01's `$1248`.
    >
    > **Net:** the literal-constant search stays closed — not because its zero was meaningful, but
    > because it is now shown incapable of returning a meaningful non-zero. The §5 partition
    > measurement is untouched. Next attempt: target a count **computed** from the size class `n`,
    > or accept the blit is outside the statically reachable code-like corpus. Free by-product:
    > `PIC64` is a byte-identical directory-scan-by-filename loader shared by all seven titles
    > (736 bytes, same offsets; load address `$4000`/`$3000`/`$0400`).
    >
    > ### SOLVED 2026-08-14 (`c64-compic-format.md` §6) — and not by finding the blit
    >
    > The 162-byte unit is **two 3x3-cell multicolour animation frames of one sprite**:
    > `[0:72]` frame A glyphs, `[72:144]` frame B glyphs, `[144:153]` frame A colour,
    > `[153:162]` frame B colour — 24x24 px per frame, one colour byte per cell. **379 files
    > decode across all seven titles**; the gallery (`renders/c64_compic/compic_gallery.png`)
    > shows unmistakable combat sprites in two poses: archers drawing bows, a coiled serpent, a
    > striding lizard-man, armoured knights with shields.
    >
    > Both earlier interpretations were wrong in an instructive way. §5.3's "two planes of the
    > same picture" are **two poses of the same creature** — animation produces exactly that
    > signature. §5.4 refuted `144 bitmap + 18 colour` by rendering it **9 cells wide**: the
    > partition was right and only the *width* was wrong, since 18 glyphs tile six ways.
    >
    > Two measurements did the work, neither of them a code search. Length-matched alphabet
    > statistics put COMPIC (**55** distinct values, entropy **4.74** in 162 bytes) on top of
    > known **pixels** (54, 4.43) and far from the solved `PIC`'s screen codes (76, 5.30) —
    > killing the "glyphs live in a companion file" hypothesis before any render was attempted.
    > And the frame length is **72 in every size class** (3.37x / 2.60x / 5.68x against a
    > closed-form permutation null) while lag `72n` sits **at or below null** (0.77x, 0.90x), so
    > an `n>1` file is a sequence of independent units, not one larger picture. Rendering `n=4`
    > as a 6x6 frame and as a 2x2 unit tiling were both tried and both failed, consistent with
    > that table.
    >
    > **Composition SOLVED the same day (`c64-compic-format.md` §6.3) — by remembering the
    > corpus has an oracle.** The remaining question was how units compose at `n=2`/`n=4`. Seam
    > statistics on the C64 side alone were suggestive but never decisive (the 48x48 candidates
    > split 11/11 even after doubling the evidence). The answer did not need C64 inference at
    > all: a COMPIC's filename hex suffix **is** the DOS block id, so `CPIC*.DAX` holds the same
    > monster, already decodable, **at a published width and height**.
    >
    > - **MON byte 153 is a shape code, not a size class.** Across 90 matched blocks in five
    >   titles, with **zero exceptions**: code 2 → DOS **24x48 tall** (36), code 3 → **48x24
    >   wide** (42), code 4 → **48x48** (22). This explains §1.2's oddity that codes 2 and 3 both
    >   meant "2 units" — they are the tall/wide split.
    > - **One ordering rule covers every shape:** units fill **column by column, right to left,
    >   top to bottom within a column**. Wide = unit 1 left, unit 0 right; tall = unit 0 above
    >   unit 1; 48x48 = `TL=2 TR=0 / BL=3 BR=1`. Frame A of each unit is one pose, frame B the
    >   other, matching the DOS `N` / `N|0x80` block pair.
    > - Ink-restricted silhouette agreement vs a cross-file null: wide **51/54** files (0.743 vs
    >   0.627), tall **32/36** (0.706 vs 0.615), 48x48 bottom row **18/18** (margin +0.299).
    >
    > ⚠️ **Reported weakness, not smoothed over:** the 48x48 **top** row wins only **12/18**
    > (margin +0.223). It is still the right reading because the disagreements are all near zero
    > (−0.141..−0.013) while every large margin is positive (+0.22..+0.76) — a wrong rule would
    > produce large negative margins and there are none. The runner-up `(0,2,3,1)` differs *only*
    > in the top row, so `test_c64_compic.py` pins the unanimous bottom row and deliberately does
    > **not** pin the top. All seven layout mutations were seen to fail before the tests were
    > trusted; two of them passed on the first attempt and were rewritten, because they restated
    > the answer as a literal instead of reading it from the module.
    >
    > **Scope:** the oracle covers **five** titles. Gateway contributes zero blocks — its DOS
    > `CPIC` frames use an item_count-3 header `parse_standard_frame` does not handle (an open
    > item, and the reason it fails loudly rather than silently). Pool of Radiance stays the
    > documented byte-153 exception and now has its own test.
    >
    > The blit routine remains unfound: the format was solved from the data alone, after two
    > consumer hunts and a constant hunt had all failed. Method note worth keeping — when a
    > consumer hunt stalls, measure the file, look at the picture, and check whether a
    > neighbouring platform already published the answer.
    >
    > ### Variable-`PIC`'s first POSITIVE predictor (2026-08-14, `c64-compic-format.md` §1.4b)
    >
    > COMPIC and CHARPIC are solved; the third family in this item, variable-size `PIC` (368
    > files), is not, and §1.4a had closed three layout readings without opening anything. It now
    > has a positive result, from a quantity the oracle had already decoded but not used — the DOS
    > block's **frame count**.
    >
    > - **A C64 `PIC` whose DOS sibling animates is ~490 bytes larger**, above the maximum of
    >   4000 label permutations (195.1), and replicated above its own null in **4 of 4 titles
    >   that can show it** (Champions +699, Death Knights +731, Curse +558, Secret +808). Gateway
    >   is genuinely uninformative — zero animated blocks. **Pool of Radiance is a real exception
    >   (+190, below its null) and is reported as one**, consistent with its role as this corpus's
    >   standing odd title.
    > - **The increment saturates at two poses.** 1→2 frames costs +405.6 (null max 219.1);
    >   **2→3-or-more costs +104.3 against a null max of 298.0**, i.e. nothing. Per-frame slope
    >   across the animated subset is **13 bytes/frame** against the ~1210 an 88x88 multicolour
    >   frame would cost. So the C64 file does **not** store the DOS frames, and a future round
    >   reading the positive result that way would be hunting eight frames that are not there.
    > - ~~That saturation is exactly what solved COMPIC does — two poses, frame A / frame B.~~
    >   ⚠️ **REFUTED the same day by §1.4c** (below): the file's own header lists up to **six**
    >   distinct frames, so the two-pose cap is not the explanation. The saturation itself stands
    >   and is sharper when re-measured against the C64's own frame count.
    > - **The rival explanation was tested.** "Animated monsters are just busier art" fails: two
    >   complexity proxies read off the same DOS pixels predict C64 length at r=0.008 and r=0.087,
    >   and stratifying on either leaves the gap intact in **every bin**, at 521/526 bytes vs the
    >   raw 491.
    > - **Not a fixed-size section:** the distributions overlap almost completely (101 of 114
    >   animated files sit inside the 1-frame range) and the SD nearly doubles, 202 → 370.
    >
    > **Next experiment this hands over**, cheaper than §1.4a's "hunt the consumer": the file is
    > expected to contain two poses, so the second pose's bytes are inside it — and the 1-frame
    > files are a **matched control group that should not contain them at all**. Diffing the two
    > populations for a length-prefixed tail, a second header pointer or a repeated glyph bank is
    > far narrower than guessing a whole-file layout, and has a built-in null.
    >
    > ### That experiment was run, and it found the header (`c64-compic-format.md` §1.4c)
    >
    > **Every conforming variable-`PIC` body opens with a 32-byte header holding a NUL-terminated,
    > zero-padded animation SEQUENCE; picture data starts at offset 32 exactly. 352 of 368 files,
    > all seven titles.** Ids are exactly `0x41`-`0x49` (`A`-`I`).
    >
    > - It is a **playback order, not a frame table** — `ABCB` (23 files) is a ping-pong loop and
    >   `CBA` (5) runs backwards, so an id can repeat. Commonest: `A` ×205, `ABC` ×32, `ABCB` ×23,
    >   `AB` ×14. Sequence length 1-7; **distinct** ids `K` = 1-6.
    > - **The frame count is now a C64-side fact**, no oracle needed, so it covers all 352
    >   conforming files rather than the 288 that pair. It is also the better predictor:
    >   `r(len, K) = 0.762` vs `r(len, DOS frames) = 0.547` (null p99 0.142).
    > - Against the DOS count on the 288 paired-and-conforming files: `K == nf` in **194**,
    >   `K < nf` in 68, `K > nf` in 26. Of 174 single-frame DOS blocks, 160 have `K = 1`.
    > - ⚠️ **This corrects the bullet struck out above.** Re-measured against `K`, the saturation
    >   is sharper (`K=1`→`K=2` +567.2 vs null max 218.5; `K=2`→`K≥3` **+10.1** vs null max
    >   273.2) — so the effect is not an artifact of the wrong frame count, only the *two-pose*
    >   explanation was wrong. Leading replacement, **untested**: DOS `PIC` frames after frame 0
    >   are XOR deltas against frame 0, so extra frames compress to almost nothing.
    > - **§1.4a's RLE negative was re-run at the corrected alignment** — it had decoded from
    >   offset 0, i.e. through 32 bytes of header. From offset 32: **239 distinct sizes vs 247 and
    >   247** for the ±1 misalignment controls, and zero hits on any expected target size. The
    >   refutation survives; the codec is still not the SSI RLE.
    > - **All 16 non-conformers identified**, not written off: `PIC64` ×7 is the known 1541
    >   directory-scan loader (6502 code in the `PIC` name space); Buck Rogers `PIC6D`/`PIC7A`-`7E`
    >   open with 484/528-byte PETSCII runs and read as text screens; `PIC3A`, `PIC4F` and `PIC41`
    >   are genuinely **unexplained** and are named as such.
    >
    > Still zero pixels decoded — the 32 bytes are a header and what follows is unread. §1.4a's
    > three refuted layouts were re-tested from offset 32 *and within each `K` group separately*
    > (so a differing per-group overhead could not smear them); all still at chance. **Next: the
    > 211 `K=1` files**, which contain one picture and no animation machinery at all — the same
    > attack-the-simplest-member move that cracked fixed-size `PIC`.
    >
    > ### The `K=1` attack landed: the file declares its own geometry (§1.4d)
    >
    > Picture data does **not** start at offset 32 — offsets 32-55 are a fixed sub-header, payload
    > starts at **56**, and four of its fields are the dimensions:
    >
    > | offset | value, all 352 conforming files | reading |
    > | --- | --- | --- |
    > | 45, 46 | `0x0b`, `0x0b` | **11 x 11 character cells = 88x88 px** |
    > | 47-48 | u16 **968** | glyph-bitmap bytes = 11·11·8 |
    > | 49-50 | u16 **121** | cell count = 11·11 |
    > | 52-53 | low byte always `$F0` | an address, destination unidentified |
    > | 54-55 | **high byte always `$D8`** | an address in C64 **colour RAM** (`$D800`-`$DBFF`) |
    >
    > **This is the point of it:** §1.4a's 88x88 was an *oracle* claim covering the 288 files that
    > pair with a DOS block. Three self-consistent fields now assert the same shape **from the C64
    > bytes alone in all 352 conforming files**, including the 32 unpaired ones and all of Buck
    > Rogers, which has no DOS `CPIC` archive at all. Control: the 37 **solved** fixed-size `PIC`
    > bodies carry scattered junk at the same offsets (`off45 ∈ {28, 68, …}`, `u16@47 ∈ {16412,
    > 8224, …}`), so the constants are a property of the format, not of the offsets chosen.
    >
    > - Offsets 32-43 are twelve bytes, 3962/4224 of them `0x01`, and they track animation hard:
    >   **179 of 211** `K=1` files are all-`01` against only **37 of 141** animated ones. Reading:
    >   per-frame timing. **Not proven** — `PIC1C` has a 2-step sequence but four non-`01` slots,
    >   which already contradicts one-slot-per-step, and that counter-example is recorded with it.
    > - **Codec still unsolved, and the negative is now sharp**: the expected output is *declared*
    >   (968+121+121 = 1210), not guessed. Both RLE polarities × four start offsets hit 1210±20 for
    >   at best 6 of 211 single-frame files — chance.
    > - **Next**, and much better targeted than "find a COMPIC blit": hunt the overlays for a store
    >   loop into `$D8xx` bounded by 121 adjacent to one bounded by 968. Checkable against the
    >   constants §5.6-§5.7 already extracted corpus-wide, so no fresh sweep is needed.
    >
    > ### First decoded section, and the reason six rounds of RLE failed (§1.4e)
    >
    > The `$D8xx` pointer was right: **the file ends in C64 colour RAM**, and the codec is
    > **literal-with-run-marker** — `c >= 0xF0` emits the *following* byte `256-c` times, anything
    > else is a literal. **SSI's RLE stores a count first; this stores a value first**, which is
    > the whole reason every attempt from §1.4a onward missed.
    >
    > **109 of 211** single-frame files end in a region decoding to values `0..15` and nothing
    > else. The band sweep is the null that matters: bands `16..31`, `32..47`, `64..79`,
    > `128..143` each score **0/211**, `0..7` scores **0**, and widening to `0..31` or `0..63`
    > adds **nothing** — the boundary is at 16 from both sides, which is the colour-RAM range
    > exactly. Byte-shuffled payloads: 0/211. The same decode at the payload's *head*: 0 files, so
    > "trailing" is measured rather than assumed.
    >
    > ⚠️ **The section length is NOT resolved**, and a surviving mutation is what exposed it:
    > 121→120 passed, so the target was swept — `N=100` fits 121 files, `N=122` fits 111, `N=121`
    > fits 109. Every byte in the region is either `<16` or a run marker, so the region is
    > homogeneous and the search finds its extent but not its start. The 121 comes from §1.4d's
    > sub-header and is *consistent with* the tail, not proven by it. That limitation now has its
    > own test, so it fails loudly if it ever stops being true.
    >
    > **Refuted on its own prediction:** deduplicated 8-byte glyph storage requires
    > `len(glyphs)/8 == max(screen)+1` — a length and a decoded value that cannot force each
    > other. **0 agree, 12 disagree, 50 of 62 glyph regions are not even a multiple of 8.**
    >
    > Glyph bitmaps and screen codes remain unread (the head decodes to 1089 for 0 of 109 files,
    > with scattered deltas — the sections do not share one stream). **Zero pixels rendered yet**,
    > so the family stays NOT solved; what changed is that one of its three sections is readable
    > and the codec family is identified for the first time.
    >
    > ### The same result with no search, and three layouts eliminated (§1.4e.1)
    >
    > Decoding the **whole payload** — no start offset, no threshold sweep, **no free parameter** —
    > and looking at the last 121 bytes beats the searched result: **155/211** vs 109/211, with
    > **211/211** payloads parsing as a complete stream (no truncated runs). Median expansion
    > 1.37x; the final 121 outputs come from a median of 80 input bytes.
    >
    > **The confound that would have made it trivial is dead: 0 of 211** files have a raw tail
    > already all `< 16`, so the codec earns every one of the 155. Band sweep still 0/211 for
    > `16..31`, `32..47`, `64..79`, `128..143`.
    >
    > ⚠️ **This test is blind to the run arithmetic** — a wrong count changes how often a byte
    > repeats, not which byte, so `all(x < 16)` scores *higher* (181/211) under `(c & 0x0F)+1`.
    > The expansion ratio is what separates them (real 1.08-1.70 vs 1.87-3.80, no overlap) and is
    > asserted for that reason; §1.4e's anchored test remains the one pinning the count.
    >
    > Three layouts eliminated, each from an independent direction:
    > - **dedup glyphs, a second way** — `(T-242) mod 8` is flat (18/28/32/25/28/27/28/25 vs ~26)
    > - **`[glyphs][screen][colour]`** — the 121 bytes before the colour block are
    >   *indistinguishable from a control window* from mid-picture (span 253 vs 252, 42 vs 47
    >   distinct); the control is what makes this a refutation rather than an observation
    > - **a longer-run opcode** — shortest third's median longest-zero-run is 15, longest third's
    >   is 12; flat, if anything inverted
    >
    > Decoded totals run 810-1715 (median 1274) with **none** at 1210, so the head genuinely emits
    > a variable byte count and does not share the tail's codec. Still zero pixels.
    >
    > ### ⚠️ The bound on all of it: the section is NOT tied to this picture (§1.4e.2)
    >
    > "Colour-RAM-ranged values" and "**this picture's** colours" are different claims. The second
    > was tested against the DOS sibling — same 88x88 artwork, so its per-cell dominant colour is
    > a second partition of the same 121 cells, and adjusted Rand index compares them without
    > needing the palettes to match. **Result: flat.** Median p **0.471** (null 0.5), 56/97 files
    > below 0.5 (null 48.5±4.9), 6 files at p≤0.059 against 5.7 expected.
    >
    > **The instrument is not blind** — inject a synthetic effect and it is caught from **12% of
    > cells** upward (8% not detected). The real data sits at the 0% row. Six cell orderings and
    > four DOS colour proxies were tried first; all flat. One proxy (`non-bg`) put 14/127 files at
    > p≤0.05 vs 6.4 expected but with median p 0.480 — a tail bump in one of four proxies tested,
    > recorded and **not** promoted to evidence.
    >
    > Two earlier baselines were wrong in opposite directions (one mismatched partner → real looked
    > 3x better; max-of-three → real looked worse). A max over k draws is not a mean; the per-file
    > empirical p-value is the unbiased form and is what the numbers above use.
    >
    > Most plausible explanation: **the C64 art is redrawn, not converted** — multicolour halves
    > horizontal resolution, so 11 cells is 44 multicolour pixels across and a direct conversion of
    > the DOS bitmap is not even possible. Which would also mean **the oracle cannot validate C64
    > pixels for this family**, only shapes and ids.
    >
    > ### The block IS a picture map — and its stride contradicts the file's own width (§1.4f)
    >
    > §1.4e.2 could not tell "the window is misplaced" from "the art is redrawn". The C64 side can,
    > because a colour map is two-dimensional and noise is not — and it comes out **positive**:
    > cells one row apart agree far above the neighbouring lags (median local excess **+0.122**,
    > **133 of 155** files at p ≤ 0.05 where chance is 7.8).
    >
    > **The null is the result.** A plain shuffle would have passed this for free — the codec's
    > output is run-heavy and shuffling destroys runs, so that null only asks "is this
    > RLE-compressible?". The null used here permutes maximal equal-value **runs**, holding the
    > histogram *and* every run length fixed and destroying only the 2-D arrangement. Its median
    > excess is −0.000. So the 121-byte window is **not** misplaced, and §1.4e.2's flat result is
    > attributable to the artwork — the first of its three stated explanations, and the survivor.
    >
    > ⚠️ **But the row stride is 12, and offset 45 declares 11.** The instrument was calibrated on
    > a map of *known* width — the DOS sibling's 11×11 dominant-colour cells, same statistic, same
    > code, same 97 rows. DOS peaks at 11 (+0.117); the C64 tail peaks at **12** (+0.071, with 11
    > at +0.013) and shows a second harmonic at 24. Both easy reconciliations are refuted: no
    > column is constant (spread 0.043, reached by 20 run-preserving null draws) and none
    > duplicates a neighbour (best adjacent pair 0.532, i.e. ordinary). The trailing all-`<16`
    > region also runs min 125 / median 136 / max 151, consistent with 12×11 = 132.
    >
    > **`968+121+121` refuted on the right prediction.** That is the C64 multicolour **bitmap**
    > layout, and §1.4e.1 killed `[glyphs][screen][colour]` using the **character-mode** prediction
    > (screen codes in a small contiguous range) — which cannot test a bitmap-mode layout at all,
    > where a screen byte is two colour nybbles spanning 0..255. Re-run properly: the screen window
    > uses 15 of 16 distinct nybbles against a mid-picture control's 15, overlaps the colour set at
    > 0.667 vs 0.643, and beats its control in only 53/155 files (34%, chance 50%). Rendering the
    > last 1210 bytes as a multicolour bitmap gives noise.
    >
    > **Next:** the `$D8xx` store-loop hunt of §1.4d should look for a bound of **132**, not 121.
    > And either the sub-header describes a source the blit re-lays-out, or offsets 45–50 are not
    > the fields §1.4d reads them as — its control shows only that those offsets are
    > format-specific, not that the reading is right. Still **zero pixels rendered**.
    >
    > All four tests mutation-checked, 7/7 killed (layout destroyed by run-preserving shuffle;
    > stride 12→11 and 12→13; calibration fed the C64 side instead of the DOS side; a constant
    > twelfth column; a duplicated twelfth column; an injected small-palette screen section).
    >
    > ### The head is not the bitmap, and the file's SIZE is tied to the picture (§1.4g)
    >
    > Same calibration trick, applied to the unread head. A C64 bitmap is cell-major, so it repeats
    > at lag 8 and 8×width; the DOS picture repacked into that order shows it (+0.0097 at 8,
    > +0.0083 at 88) and **the C64 head shows nothing** (−0.0007, +0.0001). Its equality also
    > decays to 0.032 by lag 30 where the DOS bitmap holds 0.17 — a picture has flat regions, the
    > head does not. So **no layout search treating the head as a raster in cell order can work**,
    > which is why §1.4e/§1.4e.1 killed four layouts in a row.
    >
    > **But it is not an opaque second layer either:** zlib ratio **0.720**, against the raw
    > payload it came from at 0.915 (DOS raw bitmap 0.650, decoded colour block 0.537). The outer
    > decode does real work; the head is a *structured, variable-length* representation.
    >
    > **First cross-platform content link for this family.** The colour section is not tied to the
    > DOS picture (§1.4e.2), but the number of BYTES is: raw payload length vs distinct 8-byte cell
    > patterns in the repacked DOS bitmap gives **r=+0.727** (permutation max 0.361), and vs its
    > zlib ratio **+0.596** (max 0.354), on the 97 single-frame files. Note the decode does *not*
    > improve it (+0.590), so this is evidence about the file, not a validation of the decode.
    >
    > ⚠️ **CORRECTION to §1.4b (§1.4g.1).** §1.4b ruled out "animated monsters are just busier art"
    > using proxies that predicted C64 length at r=0.008 and r=0.087 — a control that cannot
    > predict the outcome cannot adjust for it, so that stratification was arithmetic, not a test.
    > Re-run with the r=+0.73 proxy on 233 paired files: gap **+580.7** unstratified, **+611/+596/
    > +580/+550** across complexity quartiles, within-bin mean **+584.3**, permutation max +156.5.
    > **The finding stands untouched in every quartile; only its defence was invalid.** Recorded
    > precisely because the conclusion did not change — the reason to fix a bad control is that it
    > was carrying no weight.
    >
    > Four tests, mutation-checked 5/5 (pairing rotated so each C64 file scores against another
    > file's picture; payload lengths shuffled; the C64 arm fed the DOS bitmap; the calibration arm
    > fed the C64 head; the head pre-compressed).
    >
    > ### Free by-product: a DOS shape census for every family (`c64-dax-oracle.md`)
    >
    > The same read-off run across all mapped DOS roots, so the next C64 graphics attempt starts
    > with its target dimensions: `HEAD` **88x40 uniform**, `BODY` **88x48 uniform**, `CBODY`
    > **24x24 uniform**, `CHEAD` 24x8..10, `PIC` 88x88, `BIGPIC` 304x120, `SPRIT` variable-width
    > x 80. Two negatives came with it:
    > - **DOS `WALLDEF` is not a picture at all** — 0 of 124 blocks parse as frame, anim array or
    >   tile strip, though all 124 decompress cleanly into just 3 distinct sizes. So the oracle
    >   never had a shape to hand C64 `WALLDEF`; that door was closed from the start, which is
    >   worth knowing after eight rounds on that family.
    > - **C64 `SPRITE` does not tile its DOS picture** — the trailer dialect is always 13 VIC
    >   blocks across all 74 paired files while DOS widths run 24..88, refuting the
    >   `ceil(w/24) x ceil(h/21)` grid reading.
    >
    > ⚠️ **The census's own null is recorded next to it:** the uniformity holds over *every* block
    > in a root, paired or not, so it is **not** evidence that C64 `HEAD` really is DOS `HEAD` — a
    > wrong id lands on 88x40 too. It does give that open question a shape-based discriminator it
    > never had. A test asserts the null explicitly, and the WALLDEF test's skip guard was rewritten
    > after review because it gated on the very count under test — it would have gone
    > green-by-skip on the day a WALLDEF block started parsing.

  - [~] **C1.6 — read each title's own MON consumer.** Attempted 2026-08-11; the premise turned
    out to be **wrong**, which is itself the result. The C64 MON record is **480 bytes on both
    CoK and DoK** (482 on disk minus the 2-byte load address; zero exceptions across 14 CoK +
    22 DoK files). The DOS records are 409 (CoK) and 216 (DoK) — deltas of +71 and +264. So the
    C64 record is **not** an unpacked DOS record for this family, and **cannot** serve as an
    oracle for DOS field offsets without a separately-proven field mapping. Consequently the
    concrete first target below is *not* settled and cannot be settled this way:
    **DoK `hp` at byte 40 vs 214 remains undetermined.** What the disassembly did prove:
    the monster name is at C64 record offset 0 with no length prefix (CoK `COM.PREP` `$0A0F`
    and DoK `COMPREP` `$0A15` run byte-identical 40-byte scrub loops via zero-page pointer
    `$4E`), and offset `0xCB` is written as the literal pointer `$40CB` into a `$0600`-based
    parameter block, i.e. graphics-pointer territory, not a stat byte. A candidate HP-subtraction
    idiom in DoK `COMBAT $227A` was found and then **refuted** — the same `$7C74/$7C75` pair is
    a paralysis counter in CoK `COMBAT $2865`. AC/THAC0/saves/hit-dice/XP: no C64 code path
    found, deliberately left out of `tools/c64_mon.py` rather than guessed in.
    `docs/engine/research/c64-mon-format.md`. ~~**Blocked on C1.9.**~~ **Unblocked, then resolved
    NEGATIVE 2026-08-12 (`e32fa90`).** `$2E9A` (CoK) / `$2E49` (DoK) were disassembled and are
    **not** the MON consumer. They compute VIC-II screen pointers: index × `$28` (40 = screen
    width in columns, not a record size), yielding `$CC00 + row*40` paired with Color RAM
    `$D800 + row*40`. `$0288` is set to `$CC` by a 35-byte VIC-bank routine that is byte-identical
    between titles and whose registers derive `$C000 + $0C00 = $CC00` arithmetically. The clincher
    is semantic, not positional: the scrub loop keeps bytes `<$40` and blanks `>=$40`, which is
    C64 **screen-code** logic, while raw MON names are ASCII (`MON01` = `42 41 41 5A` = "BAAZ") —
    aimed at the `$4000` buffer it would blank every letter of every name. It never touches
    `$4000`. **The 2026-08-11 claim that this loop is consumer-proof of the name field at offset 0
    is RETRACTED**; the raw-byte observation of the name still stands on its own.
    **The question is still open, one step further back:** something must write text *into* those
    `$CC00` rows before the scrub clears them, and if that step reads `MON<hex>` data it is the
    first real MON-buffer consumer this project will have found. Nothing found yet.
    ~~Also note: `tools/c64_disk.py`'s `load_address()` docstring claims DOS/C64 payloads are
    "byte-identical from offset 2 onward" as a general rule — **false for the MON family**;
    that docstring needs scoping.~~ **Done 2026-08-12** (`33e7e5c`): the docstring is scoped, and
    a regression test now pins the MON record-length disagreement (C64 480 on both titles; DOS
    409 on Champions, 216 on Death Knights) so the claim cannot silently return.

    > **Round 8 addendum — the trailer-byte-3 correlation, re-checked against the right family.**
    > Round 8 landed the SPRITE trailer-byte-3 finding as part of the same commit. Auditing it
    > afterwards rather than taking the green suite as verification: all four per-title numbers and
    > the Fisher-combined `p ≈ 6.6×10⁻⁶` reproduce exactly. But its multiple-comparisons defence
    > compared that COMBINED statistic to `0.05/51`, the threshold for §14.3's family of 51
    > **per-title** correlations — a family the combined statistic was never a member of. Running
    > the check that framing implies: combine every trailer position, not just the selected one.
    > Four of the 16 are degenerate in all titles, so the family is **12**; byte 3 clears
    > `0.05/12 ≈ 4.2×10⁻³` by ~**630×**, and the runner-up (byte 4, `1.2×10⁻²`) does **not** clear
    > it at all — so the finding is not one of several candidates crowding a threshold. Byte 3 is
    > also the only sign-unanimous position, recorded as a distinguishing property rather than
    > evidence (~1.5 unanimous positions are expected among 12 by chance). The conclusion was
    > right; the argument for it was not, and is now pinned by a test that asserts the runner-up
    > *fails* as well as the winner passing. Also re-derived independently and confirmed from the
    > same commit: Gateway's 14 `WALLDEF` ids with 12 cross-side duplicated, and Side 4's GEO set
    > `08/0B/0C/0D`.
    >
    > Corollary to this round's rule: **a Bonferroni threshold is only as good as the family it
    > names.** Quoting a correction factor is not the same as correcting for the search you did.

    > **Round 10 (2026-08-14) — the first interior structure in COMPIC, and a negative that had
    > to be corrected after it was already committed.** Scope was C1.10 (COMPIC, 754 files,
    > 55.2% of the C64 art corpus). Two commits, the second correcting the first.
    >
    > What holds (`c64-compic-format.md` §5.1–§5.3, unaffected by the correction below): the
    > single-class 162-byte body partitions as **`72 | 72 | 18`** — period 72 at **3.37×** a
    > closed-form permutation null while lag 81 scores **0.71×, below its own null** (refuting
    > the natural "two 81-byte screen+colour maps" reading by analogy with the solved fixed-size
    > `PIC`); the periodicity is bounded to exactly `body[0:72] ↔ body[72:144]`; and the two
    > blocks are **planes of the same picture**, 0.415 within a file vs **0.156** across an
    > exhaustive 52,212-pair cross-file null, never identical in any of 229 bodies. The
    > *interpretation* of the 72 as `9 cells × 8 bytes` was **refuted by rendering** — nine
    > COMPICs, three size classes, hires and multicolour, all noise.
    >
    > **The correction, and the reason it is the round's real content.** The `72|72|18` partition
    > gave the blit hunt three discriminating constants the earlier consumer hunts never had. I
    > searched 446 code-like files for counted loops of those lengths, found zero at 162 and no
    > file carrying both a 72-loop and an 18-loop, and **committed that as a strong negative**
    > (`6036ffb`) on the reasoning that an over-inclusive scan returning zero is strong.
    > Measuring the baseline it had never been compared against dissolved both zeros (`0f82e36`):
    > - 4,076 counted loops corpus-wide, but **66.1% of bounds are below 32**. In the window
    >   150–174 there are 16 loops total and **16 of the 24 non-162 values are also exactly
    >   zero**. Expected count at 162 is ~0.67 — any 162-byte format shows this.
    > - Exactly **one** file corpus-wide carries a 72-loop, so expected co-occurrence with the
    >   18-loop is **0.038 files**; and **43.5%** of all value pairs co-occur in zero files. Zero
    >   was the modal outcome, never in doubt.
    > - Every surviving hit is a **CBM system constant, not a format constant**. The corpus's
    >   most-shared counted loop looked like the lead of the round — `PIC64`'s `CPY #$12` at body
    >   offset 130, byte-identical in all seven titles, in a file whose name says "picture", 7 of
    >   17 18-loop holders against 2.3% of other files. The disassembly puts it inside a **1541
    >   directory scan** (`CMP #$82` entry type, `LDA $03FD,Y` filename compare, `CPX #$08`
    >   entries/sector, `ADC #$20` entry size), so its 18 is a *filename field* length — the same
    >   failure as GDRIVE01's `$1248` two sections earlier.
    >
    > The search stays closed for a better reason than published: not that its zero was
    > meaningful, but that the method is **incapable of returning a meaningful non-zero** at this
    > corpus size, because every numeric coincidence with a format length resolves to a
    > ubiquitous CBM/VIC constant.
    >
    > One genuine by-product, pinned separately: **`PIC64` is a byte-identical
    > directory-scan-by-filename loader shared by all seven titles** — 736 bytes, same code at
    > the same offsets, differing only in load address (`$4000` in five, `$3000` in Curse and
    > Gateway, `$0400` in Pool of Radiance).
    >
    > Rule this round adds, extending round 9's: **a zero result is a statistic and needs a null
    > as much as a ratio does.** "Over-inclusive, therefore a strong negative" is not sufficient —
    > over-inclusiveness only removes the false-negative worry and says nothing about
    > discriminating power. Before publishing "we searched and found none," measure how often the
    > search finds anything at all, and specifically in the neighbourhood of the tested value.

  - [x] **C1.9 — SOLVED 2026-08-12. The "always-resident low-memory kernel" is `LIBRARY`,
    relocated to `$2DC8`, with `LINKER` at `$2D00` as the overlay dispatcher.** It is an
    ordinary directory file after all; what hid it is that it does **not** load at the `$4000`
    address in its own PRG header. `SETLFS` with **secondary address 0** selects a *relocated*
    load, so the caller's address wins and the file header is ignored. Both premises below —
    "not a file on any disk side" and "hidden outside the directory" — were wrong, and the two
    ways in proposed below were the right two: (a) detokenizing `BOOT` is what produced the
    answer.

    Two agents converged independently, and the lead session verified both on raw bytes rather
    than by re-running their tools:
    - **Structural.** A census-scored origin sweep over all internal JSR targets picks `$2DC8`
      for LIBRARY at 19/48 against a next-best of 9 in Champions, and 20/55 against 10 in Death
      Knights.
    - **Literal.** The `$0801` boot stub (`BOOT` on Champions, `DEATH KNIGHTS` on Death Knights)
      is tokenized CBM BASIC V2 — which is exactly why it "disassembles as incoherent 6502 from
      byte 0" below. Detokenized, at identical line numbers in both titles, it contains
      `SYS 11720` = **`$2DC8`** (line 41) and `SYS 11520` = **`$2D00`** (line 240), with
      `SYS 65466`/`65469`/`65493` (`$FFBA` SETLFS / `$FFBD` SETNAM / `$FFD5` LOAD) in its loader
      subroutines. The two origins derived structurally are also literal constants in the shipped
      program.

    All ten previously-unexplained JSR targets listed below fall inside LIBRARY's span in
    **both** titles. Docs: `docs/engine/research/c64-resident-kernel.md` (what and where) and
    `docs/engine/research/c64-boot-chain.md` (how it gets there). Tools: `tools/c64_kernel.py`,
    `tools/c64_boot.py`.

    > **Why the earlier page-aligned sweep missed it — corrected here, because the lead session
    > ran that sweep and has the measurements.** The agents' account blamed cross-title
    > conflation of the 10-address target list; that is not what happened (all ten land inside
    > LIBRARY in both titles, so the filter never rejected it). The real cause is **sample size**:
    > at the true origin the "preceded by RTS/JMP/RTI" heuristic scores only **4 of 10** in
    > Champions and **1 of 10** in Death Knights, against 3 of 10 at page-aligned `$2E00` and 3
    > of 10 at `$2700`. Ten targets cannot separate signal from noise; the census sweep that won
    > used 48 and 55. The lesson for the next structural sweep in this project is **"collect more
    > targets", not "align more finely"** — non-page-alignment was real but secondary.

    Still open, downstream: `FINAL` is named in both titles' dispatch tables but corresponds to
    no file on any side; who loads `STOP.PRG`; the roles of `SECSET02`/`SECSET10`/`SECSET64`;
    LIBRARY's ~7.4KB interior is unmapped; DoK's `CODE00/01/03` uninvestigated; `GDRIVE05`
    undocumented; ~27 of GDRIVE00's table slots untraced; COMBAT2's real origin unsettled. The
    GDRIVE01 sprite-caller (the C1.8 lead below) is **still unlocated** — the COMBAT `$C015`
    lead was refuted this round, those calls resolve against GDRIVE00.

    <details><summary>Original C1.9 writeup (2026-08-11), retained — its diagnosis was right and
    its premises were wrong</summary>

    This is the single highest-value C64 item, and it was found the honest
    way — **three of the four 2026-08-11 slices hit it independently, without knowing about each
    other**, from three different directions:
    - C1.6 (MON): the routine that sets zero-page pointer `$4E/$4F` before the name-scrub loop
      is `JSR $2E9A` (CoK) / `JSR $2E49` (DoK). Until it is readable, we cannot tell whether MON
      fields are ever read from the raw `$4000` load buffer at all — which is the load-bearing
      missing link for every further field trace.
    - C1.8 COMPIC: `GDRIVE00` calls `$2E04`/`$2E25`; `GDRIVE02` calls `$2E84`/`$30E2`/`$3B69`/
      `$3B70`.
    - C1.8 SPRITE/WALLSET: the GDRIVE01 parameter-block caller is absent from every overlay
      searched, consistent with living here.

    **The region is roughly `$2E00`-`$3C00` and it is not among the ~600 PRG directory entries
    on any of CoK's 6 sides.** `BOOT` (1331 bytes, loads at `$0801`) disassembles as incoherent
    6502 from byte 0 — consistent with a tokenized BASIC stub, and far too small to be the kernel
    itself. Two ways in, neither tooled yet: (a) BASIC-detokenize `BOOT` to see what it actually
    `LOAD`s, or (b) read tracks/sectors outside the standard 1541 directory — a well-known period
    copy-protection technique that would hide a file from `c64_disk.directory()` entirely. Note
    `tools/c64_disk.py` already walks raw sectors, so (b) is mostly a matter of scanning
    unallocated chains rather than new low-level code.

    > **Correction landed with this item (lead session, 2026-08-11) — a cross-slice contradiction
    > neither per-slice verifier could see.** Two agents assigned `GDRIVE00` two different
    > residences: `$C000` (COMPIC) and `$4000` (WALLSET, following the scout's own weak guess).
    > `$C000` is correct, but **the COMPIC agent's stated reason was invalid** — it cited a
    > "coherent full disassembly at `--org 0xC000`", and `c64_disasm.py`'s byte decode is
    > *identical at every origin* (the origin only shifts the printed address column), so that
    > check cannot distinguish anything. The scout's handoff warned about this exact trap.
    > Re-derived three ways that can each fail: GDRIVE00's 35 table targets (`$C157`-`$CAB4`) all
    > land inside its own body at `$C000` (`$C000`-`$CAF5`) and all land outside it at `$4000`;
    > restricting to the 10 slots that actually discriminate (`$C04B`-`$C066`, the entries
    > GDRIVE01's 25-entry table does not also cover) gives a stable 6 hits in *both* titles; and
    > the `$4000` hypothesis gives 7 hits in CoK but **zero** in DoK despite GDRIVE00 being
    > byte-identical between them — the signature of coincidental alignment, not residence.
    > **Consequence:** the WALLSET doc's `JSR $403D` byte-reuse finding is retracted, and its
    > open question "what occupies `$CA00`-`$CAB4`" is answered — GDRIVE00's own code.

    </details>
